segments.t: Hearing Fedya's story, Nastya scolds him and insists that her husband Kostya has a spotless browser history, while across town Chef Barinov and Elena sit through an awful comedy trailer.
Ты у Кости историю браузера проверь.
Вы просто совсем не в теме.
Let's walk through each line of Nastya's reaction and the cinema scene.
'Ugh, Fedya, how vulgar you are!' The noun denotes a person who tells tacky, vulgar jokes.
Ты у Кости историю браузера проверь.
'Check Kostya's browser history on his laptop.' Modern tech terms like 'browser' and 'laptop' decline just like regular Russian masculine nouns.
'I already checked his laptop.' Nastya uses the feminine imperfective past tense to state that she has checked it before.
'There is nothing bad on there.' After 'nothing', any descriptive adjective takes the genitive singular ending '-ogo'.
'That means he simply deleted it.' Fedya teases her with the perfective past tense of 'to delete'.
'I will stay out in the corridor for a bit.' Adding the prefix 'po-' to 'will be' means 'I will stay for a short while'.
'I will wait until the trailer finishes.' In Russian, clauses with 'until' ('poka') include the negative particle 'ne' before the future verb.
'What, is everything really that bad?' Three simple words ask whether the movie preview is really that terrible.
'A question has come up for me here.' Literally 'a question stood up/arose', this is a standard phrase for 'I have a question'.
'A nightmare, this is aimed at fools.' The neuter short-form participle 'calculated/designed for' takes the preposition 'on' plus the accusative.
Вы просто совсем не в теме.
'You are simply out of the loop.' Literally 'in the theme', this slang phrase means to be 'in the know' or 'hip to it'.
'It is impossible to watch such a movie.' The predicative adverb 'impossible' pairs with the imperfective infinitive 'to watch'. Now listen to the whole conversation again at natural speed.
Ты у Кости историю браузера проверь.
Вы просто совсем не в теме.
Pay special attention to how Russian expresses 'until it finishes': the word for 'while' combines with 'not' before the perfective future verb. See you in the next scene.
